title: At the deathbed
hook: beside the dying, the words la ilaha illallah are said gently, so they can be the last

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering death, and your line: remember the end. When something felt huge, did the line shrink it? Today, from remembering the end to standing beside it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

The room is quiet. A machine beeps somewhere, or a clock ticks, or there's only breathing. Family sits close. Someone holds a hand. And at some point, in Muslim homes and hospital rooms, someone leans in near the one who is dying and says, softly, a single line. La ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. Not loudly. Not as a command. Just said near them, so they might hear it, and say it too. It's the line at the heart of the faith, and the hope is that it will be the last they hear and say.
screen: `THE ROOM IS QUIET.` → `SOMEONE LEANS IN.` → `LET IT BE THE LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: The practice comes from a short hadith in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in paraphrase: prompt your dying ones to say la ilaha illallah. The Arabic word for this prompting is talqin, gently putting words on someone's tongue. And a hadith in Abu Dawud gives the hope behind it: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden. That's why the line is said there. Not as a test the dying person has to pass. As a gift, offered at the door. Some scholars advised doing it with great gentleness: say it near them rather than ordering them to repeat it, and if they say it once, don't keep pressing. The dying are tired. The words are meant to comfort, not to burden. Sahih Muslim keeps another instruction for that room, from Umm Salamah. When you are with the sick or the dying, the Prophet said, in paraphrase, say good things, because the angels say amen to whatever you say. So the room is watched over, and the words in it matter. Then, when death comes, there's a line from the Qur'an that Muslims say. In Pickthall's translation of surah al-Baqarah: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." The first line said beside the bed is about Allah alone. The line said after is about where the person has gone. Between them, a family keeps its voice low and its words good.
screen: `PROMPT YOUR DYING: LA ILAHA ILLALLAH.` · `TALQIN: GENTLY, NOT PRESSING.` · `SAY GOOD THINGS; ANGELS SAY AMEN.` · `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the words to say. Settle, and breathe. If you're learning, simply listen to the line, and if you pray, you can say it with your breath. La ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. Slowly, softly, as if to someone you love who is very tired. Let it settle. Then the second line, for after: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. We are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning. Say each one a few times, quietly, until the words feel familiar in your mouth. The bell holds the time.
At the deathbed. Saying la ilaha illallah gently near the dying, speaking only good, and afterward, unto Him we are returning. Today's word.
Your line: say it softly to them. Today, say the two lines once more on your own, so they're ready if you ever need them. Tomorrow, washing the body. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: At a deathbed, Muslim family members gently say la ilaha illallah near the dying person, without pressing them to repeat it, and after death they say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.

fork.setup: you're beside someone dying. they've said la ilaha illallah once, and they're very tired. what now?
options: keep asking them to repeat it.
stop pressing, stay close, and speak only good.
leave the room so they can rest.
fork.reveal: the talqin is gentle: once said, don't press; and in Muslim, say good things, for the angels say amen.

original.note: Arabic: prompting, gently putting the words before the dying.

trapdoor: what you thought: at a Muslim deathbed people recite prayers for the dying.
what it means: someone gently says la ilaha illallah near them, so it can be their last word, and the room speaks only good.
what a scholar hears: the talqin hadith in Sahih Muslim, the last-words hadith in Abu Dawud, and Umm Salamah's report of the angels saying amen.
